title: AMD Acquires Taalas to Etch AI Models Directly Into Custom Silicon
excerpt: The Toronto-based startup claims its chips deliver 1,000x more efficient inference by hard-coding neural network weights into specialized processors, marking AMD's fourth AI acquisition in under a year.
body:
• AMD has acquired Toronto-based Taalas, which develops technology to etch AI models directly into custom silicon, delivering what it claims is 1,000x greater efficiency than software-based inference.
  • Taalas had raised $219 million in total funding since emerging from stealth in 2024, and its HC1 chip claims to outperform Nvidia's H200 and B200 on tokens per second while using one-tenth the power.
  • The deal is AMD's fourth AI acquisition in under a year, following MK1, MEXT, and FastFlowLM, as it builds a full-stack inference platform.
  • The acquisition intensifies competition with Nvidia, which bought Groq's inference technology in March, signaling that the AI chip war has shifted decisively from training to deployment.

Advanced Micro Devices said Thursday it would acquire Taalas, a Toronto-based chip startup that embeds AI models directly into custom silicon, in an undisclosed deal that marks AMD's most aggressive move yet in the race to dominate AI inference computing.

Taalas develops specialized processors that hard-code neural network weights into mask ROM fabric paired with SRAM, eliminating the memory bottlenecks that slow conventional GPU-based inference. The approach yields what the company claims is a 1,000-fold improvement in computational efficiency over running models on general-purpose hardware.

A New Approach to AI Silicon

Founded in August 2023 by Ljubisa Bajic — a former architect at both AMD and Nvidia and co-founder of Tenstorrent — Taalas emerged from stealth in early 2024 with a radical thesis: instead of simulating AI on general-purpose processors, cast the intelligence directly into the chip itself.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=RY4vzqEP27U

"We should not be simulating intelligence on general purpose computers, but casting intelligence directly into silicon. Implementing deep learning models in silicon is the straightest path to sustainable AI."

— Ljubisa Bajic, Taalas CEO

The company's HC1 Technology Demonstrator, fabricated by TSMC on its 6nm process node and optimized for Meta's Llama 3.1 8B model, claims to generate more tokens per second per user than Nvidia's H200 and B200 GPUs, as well as hardware from Groq, SambaNova, and Cerebras — all while consuming roughly one-tenth the power at 200 watts per card.

Each chip runs a single model, with only two metal layers needing customization for each new deployment. The turnaround from model weights to working silicon takes approximately two months, according to the company, at a fraction of what training that model costs.

AMD's Inference Acquisition Spree

The Taalas deal is AMD's fourth AI-focused acquisition since November 2025, when it bought MK1, an inference software startup. The company added MEXT in June and FastFlowLM in July to its Artificial Intelligence Group, building out what it calls a "full-stack AI platform."

AMD plans to integrate Taalas's technology into its accelerator roadmap alongside its Instinct GPU line, according to Vamsi Boppana, senior vice president of AMD's AI Group. "AMD is building a full-stack AI platform that gives customers the flexibility to deploy the right compute solutions for every AI workload," Boppana said in a statement.

Taalas had raised $219 million in total funding, including a $169 million round in February 2026, before the acquisition. The startup's engineering team, led by co-founders Drago Ignjatovic and Lejla Bajic alongside CEO Ljubisa Bajic, will join AMD.

The Inference Battleground

The acquisition underscores a broader industry shift. As AI deployment scales from research labs to production applications — chatbots, code assistants, real-time translation — the economics of inference have become the central battlefield for chipmakers.

Nvidia moved first in March, unveiling a new processor built on technology from Groq, another inference-focused startup. Google continues to develop its custom TPU chips. The common thread: inference workloads now dwarf training in total compute demand, and the companies that can deliver the cheapest tokens per second will capture the bulk of AI infrastructure spending.

For AMD, which has steadily gained AI market share but still trails Nvidia by a wide margin, Taalas represents a potential differentiator. If the technology scales beyond single-model chips to support larger frontier models, it could fundamentally alter the cost structure of AI deployment.

What to Watch

AMD has not disclosed financial terms or a timeline for integrating Taalas's technology into commercial products. The key question is whether the model-specific chip approach — essentially an AI cartridge system — can scale to the massive parameter counts of frontier models like GPT-5 or Llama 4, or whether it remains most effective for smaller, high-volume deployment models. Wall Street will be watching AMD's next earnings call for clarity on how quickly Taalas silicon moves from lab to data center.
